newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines internet set to mushroom.
newsitem.headline: Philippines internet set to mushroom.

text.p: Internet use in the Philippines is set to mushroom over the coming year as more people gain access to computers and telephone lines, industry officials said.

"Prospects for growth in the Internet business here are tremendous," said Julie Figueroa, managing director of Infocom Technologies Inc. "Internet connectivity will definitely increase by a minimum of 300 percent by next year."
Analysts estimate there are currently some 20,000 internet users in the Philippines.
Figueroa was speaking at a ceremony announcing the purchase of a 51 percent stake in Infocom by the Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co. (PLDT).
Infocom officials said PLDT's majority stake in Infocom, the country's largest internet service provider, would trigger a new and aggressive marketing campaign.

"The other ISPs (Internet Service Providers) are also aggressively marketing and we have not been marketing for almost six months now, but with the venture in place, we are finalising our business plans," Infocom President Renato Gendrano said.
PLDT is the Philippines' dominant telecommunications firm controlling more than 80 percent of the telecoms' market.
Officials from both firms declined to say how much PLDT had paid for the majority stake in Infocom, a local affiliate of New Jersey-based Sequel Concept Inc.
Figueroa said the laying of a large number of new telephone lines would open big opportunities for Internet growth.

"The 300 percent figure is a good forecast. Telecom firms tying up with Internet providers has been the order of the day, and this just goes to show the increased demand," Communications Undersecretary Josefina Lichauco told Reuters.
In a three-year programme that began last year, the government hopes to provide four to five million new telephone lines.
The government secured commitments from several firms to lay the lines in exchange for licences to run lucrative cellular telephone and international gateway services.
Lichauco said access to telephones would rise to 10 per 100 persons by 1998 from two per 100 at present.
Simeon Kintanar, head of the regulatory National Telecommunications Commission, said that legal reforms had made it easier to set up a company providing Internet services.
The Public Telecommunications Act passed last year deregulated the telecoms value-added services category that includes the Internet.
Prior to passage of the law, ISPs had to secure a franchise from Congress and a certificate of public convenience and necessity.
The number of ISPs in the Philippines grew from less than 10 to 79 at present following the easing of the restrictions.
